distress-tolerance/actions-based-on-valu.note: Values clarify which alternative behavior is worth the cost of change.
Once you accept what you can't change, channel the freed energy into a value-based proactive plan.
Once the body is calmer, re-engage with what matters instead of the urge.
Willingness opens you to effective action; your values point to which action.

distress-tolerance/half-smile.note: Half Smile is the body-based way to practice non-resistance while you accept.
A gentler body-based option when full TIPP is too much or unavailable.
Soften the body with a half smile while you ride the wave.

distress-tolerance/urge-surfing.note: ACCEPTS distracts away from the wave; urge surfing rides it — opposite mechanisms for the same urge.
This decides a behavior is not worth it; urge surfing is how you ride out the urge without acting on it.
Distraction moves attention away from the urge; urge surfing stays with it — opposite strategies for the same urge.
Soften the body with a half smile while you ride out an urge.
RESISTT manages the urge by shifting away from it; urge surfing sits with it — opposite mechanisms.

distress-tolerance/resistt.note: Both are multi-tool distraction toolkits for surviving the moment — pick one per situation.
This prepared list is the raw material for RESISTT's "Engage in a distracting activity" step.
When very activated, use active distraction (RESISTT) first, then self-soothe as intensity drops.

distress-tolerance/tipp.note: TIPP is a momentary rescue; values-based action is the long game that reduces how often crises arise.
TIPP is fast and in-the-moment; this is slow and deliberative — choose by whether you are calm enough to think.
Grounding reorients attention without the physiological jolt of TIPP — a gentler route when the body isn't in full alarm.
Acute bodily arousal is the signal for the fastest body-based down-regulation.
TIPP jolts the body to down-regulate fast; self-soothing gently comforts — choose by how intense the arousal is.
A cold-temperature jolt (TIPP's ice cube) can steady you while you surf a strong urge.

distress-tolerance/cost-benefit-analysis.note: Later, when calm, analyze whether the crisis behavior you spotted here is worth changing.
After the crisis passes, if it was driven by a recurring behavior, analyze it while calm to prevent the next one.

distress-tolerance/self-soothing.note: Both are gentle activity-based ways through distress; self-soothing targets the senses to calm, distraction shifts focus.
Both calm through the senses — grounding reorients to present reality, self-soothing adds pleasant sensory comfort.

distress-tolerance/radical-acceptance.note: Use ACCEPTS until intensity decreases, then shift to Radical Acceptance.
Accept what you can't change, then invest the freed energy in what you value.
The body-calm of a half smile opens the door to accepting what you can't change.
Once the urge is handled, move from surviving toward accepting what you cannot change.
You radically accept the facts first; willingness is the flexible stance you then take toward them.

distress-tolerance/recognize-emotional-c.note: Feed the crisis behaviors you identified there in as the behavior to analyze here.

distress-tolerance/willingness-vs-willfu.note: Willingness is the open stance; your values supply the direction to act in.
You must accept the facts before you can willingly, flexibly work with them.

distress-tolerance/accepts.note: ACCEPTS's "Activities" category draws on the same prepared list.
Both are multi-tool distraction toolkits for surviving the moment — learn both, choose one per situation.
ACCEPTS resets the mind by distraction where TIPP resets the body — choose by whether the crisis feels somatic or cognitive.
After surfing the peak, distraction (ACCEPTS) can carry you the rest of the way down.

distress-tolerance/grounding.note: Both are quiet, low-effort, present-moment ways to settle without physiological intervention.
Cognitive spiral (not bodily arousal) calls for reorienting to the present.
Both work through the senses — grounding reorients to the present, self-soothing adds comforting sensory input.

distress-tolerance/distracting-activitie.note: Grounding turns attention toward present sensory reality; distraction turns it away toward an activity.
When the warning sign is an urge to act, buy time by distracting away from it.
The "Engage in a distracting activity" step draws directly on your prepared distraction list.
Both are gentle activity-based routes through distress; soothing calms via the senses, distraction shifts focus.
